title: The Curé of Ars (1786–1859)
hookLine: a struggling student priest who, his biographers say, came to spend up to sixteen hours a day hearing confessions

lines: A STUDENT WHO FAILS THE LATIN.
cards: A seminary student in France cannot get the Latin to stay in his head. Lectures and exams are all in Latin. He is older than the others, a farmer's son, and he fails.
A local priest takes him on as a private pupil and keeps him going, more out of trust than results. Ordained at last, he is sent to a small, quiet village called Ars.

His biographers remember the vicar general telling him there was not much love of God in that parish, and that he would put some there. Within his lifetime, people came from far away and waited hours, sometimes days.
Not for his Latin: to kneel in a small wooden box and talk to him.

teach.h: A SLOW START, A STUBBORN PRAYER.
teach.b: His name was Jean-Marie Vianney, and Catholics know him as the Curé of Ars; curé is French for a parish priest. First, the slow start. He was no scholar, and he knew it.
What he had was stubbornness and prayer. He spent long hours in his church, and went house to house to know the village's farm families. Second, the box.
The confessional is where a Catholic tells a priest their sins and hears the words of absolution, forgiveness given in God's name.

teach.h: THE BOX: SIXTEEN HOURS A DAY.
teach.b: His early biographers say that in his later years he sat there up to sixteen hours a day.

teach.h: I LOOK AT HIM, HE LOOKS AT ME.
teach.b: Tradition says he slept little and ate plainly to keep going. People came because, they said, he listened, and seemed to understand them. Third, a farmer in the back pew.

As the story goes, an old man sat in the church for long stretches without moving his lips. Asked what he did there, he answered that he looked at God and God looked at him. The Curé loved that answer, and repeated it.
The Church later named him patron of parish priests. Not brilliant ones; ordinary ones in ordinary places.

teach.h: UPON ONE SINNER THAT DOTH PENANCE.
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims, Jesus tells of a shepherd who leaves the flock to find one lost sheep, and says there shall be joy in heaven "upon one sinner that doth penance." One.
The Curé of Ars spent his life on the one in front of him.

how: Catholics go to confession, the sacrament of penance, at their parish, often on Saturdays or before Mass; many parishes add extra hours in Lent and Advent, and priests keep the Curé of Ars's feast on August 4.

practice: Many Catholics take a day like this as a nudge toward confession; whatever your path, let one thing surface that you'd rather not look at, a word said, a thing left undone, and name it quietly to yourself.
If you pray, bring that one thing to God; if you don't, let it be seen, and breathe out.
